question: A company runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL production DB instances on the db.r6i instance class and expects to resize them several times within that instance class over the next 3 years. It wants Reserved DB instance discounts to keep applying after each resize. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Purchase Reserved DB instances for db.r6id.large so they can apply to any r6 instance class variant.
Purchase db.r6i Reserved DB instances in the same Region, because size flexibility applies across db.r6i sizes.
Purchase RDS for SQL Server License Included Reserved DB instances, which are the only size-flexible type.
Purchase the Reserved DB instances in a cheaper Region, because the discount applies in any Region.
explanation: Size-flexible Reserved DB instances apply automatically across all sizes of the same instance class type in the same Region and engine for RDS for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Db2, and Oracle BYOL, using normalized units. They do not apply across different class types such as db.r6id, size flexibility does not apply to SQL Server or Oracle License Included, and reservations are tied to a Region.

question: A company wants its analytics AWS account to create a fast, storage-efficient copy of a production Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster that is owned by a different account. The production cluster is encrypted with the default AWS managed key for RDS (aws/rds). Which steps are required? (Select THREE.)
options: Share the aws/rds key with the analytics account by editing its key policy.
Re-create the production cluster with a customer managed KMS key by copying a snapshot with that key and restoring it.
Export the cluster to Amazon S3 and grant the analytics account read access to the bucket.
Share the cluster with the analytics account by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
Enable Backtrack on the production cluster so that the analytics account can rewind its clone.
Add the analytics account to the key policy of the customer managed KMS key.
explanation: Cross-account Aurora cloning uses AWS RAM to share the cluster, after which the other account creates a copy-on-write clone. A cluster encrypted with the default RDS key cannot be cloned cross-account, so it must first be re-created with a customer managed key (snapshot copy with the new key, then restore), and that key must be shared with the other account through its key policy. The AWS managed aws/rds key cannot be shared, and an S3 export is not a clone.

question: A company runs Amazon RDS for MySQL with automated backups enabled. The business asks how much recent data could be lost if the team must recover from logical corruption by using point-in-time restore. Which statement is correct?
options: Only one automated snapshot is taken per day during the backup window, so up to 24 hours of changes can be lost.
Point-in-time restore can return the database only to the exact creation time of a manual or automated snapshot.
RDS uploads transaction logs to S3 every 5 minutes, so the latest restorable time is usually within 5 minutes.
Point-in-time restore overwrites the existing DB instance in place and replays the logs, so no data is lost.
explanation: RDS uploads transaction logs for DB instances to Amazon S3 every five minutes, so a point-in-time restore can usually go to within about the last 5 minutes (the LatestRestorableTime) anywhere in the retention period. Restores are not limited to snapshot times, and a point-in-time restore always creates a new DB instance rather than overwriting the source.

question: A company moved all of its Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL clusters to Aurora I/O-Optimized. Six months later, cost reports show that one reporting cluster performs very little I/O; under Aurora Standard pricing, its I/O charges would be about 5% of its total Aurora spend. What should the solutions architect recommend for this cluster?
options: Keep Aurora I/O-Optimized, because it is always the cheaper configuration for clusters with low I/O.
Add Aurora Replicas so that the I/O charges are spread across more DB instances.
Switch the cluster's storage configuration to Aurora Standard.
Convert the cluster to an RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB cluster to remove I/O charges.
explanation: AWS recommends Aurora I/O-Optimized when I/O spending is 25% or more of total Aurora spending and Aurora Standard when it is less than 25%, so this low-I/O cluster should move to Aurora Standard; switching from I/O-Optimized to Standard is allowed at any time. Adding replicas adds instance cost, and migrating to a different engine deployment is unnecessary effort.

question: A manufacturer runs a packaged application whose vendor requires installing a third-party agent and changing operating system settings on the Microsoft SQL Server database host. The company wants AWS to automate backups and point-in-time recovery and does not want to take on all database administration itself. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon RDS for SQL Server with a custom option group
Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL
SQL Server on Amazon EC2 managed with AWS Systems Manager
Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server
explanation: RDS Custom for SQL Server gives privileged access to the database and the underlying operating system so customers can install agents and customize the host, while AWS still automates tasks such as automated backups and point-in-time recovery. Standard RDS does not allow host access, Babelfish changes the database engine, and SQL Server on EC2 leaves all database management to the customer.

question: A Java application connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster through the cluster endpoint. After a failover that RDS reported as complete within 35 seconds, the application kept failing to connect for a long time until the JVM was restarted. What should the solutions architect do to prevent this?
options: Set the JVM DNS cache TTL (networkaddress.cache.ttl) to 60 seconds or less.
Connect to the instance endpoint of the writer DB instance instead of the cluster endpoint to avoid DNS changes.
Increase the backup retention period on the DB cluster so that failover completes faster.
Turn off semisynchronous replication between the writer and readers to shorten the failover time.
explanation: Failover changes the DNS record behind the endpoint to point to the promoted reader, but some JVM configurations cache DNS lookups indefinitely, so the application keeps using the old IP address. AWS recommends a JVM TTL of no more than 60 seconds. Instance endpoints do not follow the writer role, backup retention does not affect failover, and replication mode is not a customer setting for this problem.

question: A company has AWS Lambda functions that query an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in private subnets. The company wants to pool database connections, avoid storing database passwords in function code or configuration, and keep the database and proxy private. Which actions should the solutions architect take? (Select THREE.)
options: Make the RDS Proxy publicly accessible so that the functions can reach it without VPC configuration.
Store the database password in Lambda environment variables encrypted with the default key.
Create an RDS Proxy in the database's VPC that retrieves the database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager.
Enable Multi-AZ on the DB instance so that each function gets its own standby connection.
Configure the functions to authenticate to the proxy by using IAM authentication.
Attach the functions to subnets in the VPC and allow their security group in the proxy's security group.
explanation: RDS Proxy pools connections, can retrieve database credentials from Secrets Manager, and can require IAM authentication from clients, so no password lives in the functions. The proxy must be in the same VPC as the database and cannot be publicly accessible, so the functions must be connected to the VPC and allowed by the proxy's security group. Environment variable passwords and Multi-AZ standbys do not meet the requirements.

question: An Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL primary DB instance uses Provisioned IOPS SSD storage to meet strict OLTP latency targets. The company is adding two read replicas for internal reports, where some latency variation is acceptable. The company wants to minimize the cost of the replicas. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Keep Provisioned IOPS storage on the replicas, because a read replica must use the same storage type as its source.
Use gp3 storage for the read replicas, because a replica's storage type can differ from the primary's.
Replace the read replicas with the existing Multi-AZ standby instance, which has no additional storage charges.
Configure the read replicas with magnetic storage, which has the lowest price per GiB of the RDS storage types.
explanation: For MySQL, MariaDB, and PostgreSQL, the storage type of a read replica is independent of the primary, and AWS gives the example of using General Purpose SSD on replicas of a Provisioned IOPS primary to reduce costs, accepting that replica performance may differ. A Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads, and magnetic storage is deprecated and no longer offered for new DB instances.

question: A company runs Amazon RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition under the Bring Your Own License model. Auditors require that selected sensitive columns be encrypted by the database engine itself, in addition to storage-level encryption, so that data files and backups are protected. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Enable RDS encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key, which also encrypts snapshots and backups.
Set rds.force_ssl to 1 in a custom DB parameter group so that data sent to and from the columns is encrypted.
Add the TDE option to a custom option group for the DB instance and use TDE column encryption.
Enable Database Activity Streams with a customer managed KMS key so that the sensitive columns are encrypted.
explanation: RDS for Oracle supports Oracle Transparent Data Encryption (TDE), which is enabled by adding the TDE option to an option group (supported only for the BYOL model); TDE column encryption encrypts individual sensitive data elements inside the database, and RDS manages the Oracle wallet and master key. Note that the TDE option is permanent once associated. RDS encryption at rest alone works at the storage level, rds.force_ssl is a PostgreSQL parameter for encryption in transit, and Database Activity Streams monitor activity rather than encrypt data.

question: An EC2-hosted reporting service must connect to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance as the database user report_ro by using IAM database authentication. IAM database authentication is already enabled on the DB instance. Which additional steps are required? (Select TWO.)
options: Attach an IAM policy to the EC2 instance role that allows rds-db:connect on the dbuser ARN for report_ro on that DB instance.
Grant the instance role the rds:ModifyDBInstance permission so that it can request authentication tokens.
Add the instance role ARN as the source of an inbound rule in the DB security group.
Create the report_ro database user so that it is identified with AWSAuthenticationPlugin.
Store the report_ro password in AWS Secrets Manager and reference the secret in the IAM policy.
explanation: IAM database authentication needs an IAM policy that allows the rds-db:connect action on the ARN arn:aws:rds-db:region:account:dbuser:DbiResourceId/db-user-name, and a database account created with IDENTIFIED WITH AWSAuthenticationPlugin for MySQL. ModifyDBInstance is unrelated to connecting, security group rules use CIDRs or security groups rather than IAM roles, and no password is used with IAM authentication.
